Nevertheless, it is important to note that the weights, denoted as \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) in Equations 18 and 19 as defined in Equation 16, are already defined as the roots of the quadratic equation [27], and they serve the purpose of strengthening the vibratory assistance of the accelerator guide rails by providing passive vibration suppression during low-speed behaviors.

If the linear acceleration parameter value \(u_0\) required for steady-state operation in the force versus displacement curve is fixed at one, as in the case of the constant \(u_0\) in Equation 14, the optimal value of parameter weight, when the PID controller output \(u_1\) is directly accessible, is \(M_{\rho i} = 2.1\) for lineal inductance mechanical system [28], and when the PID controller output \(u_1\) is variable, the optimal value of is either 4 or 3, for sinusoidal and three-phase permanent magnet synchronous machines [29], respectively.

### 4.2 Parametric Analysis and Impact of Wheel Dynamics

In this subsection, the impact of wheel dynamics on the effectiveness of the linear acceleration PID performance controller is explored, and the corresponding analysis results are provided. Additionally, an improvement in efficiency is suggested, which implies that the dynamics of the wheel only becomes a factor of 0.0001 relative to the torque or acceleration [30, 31, 32].

### 4.2.1 Development and Implementation of Linear Acceleration PID Performance Controller

The linear acceleration PID performance controller is developed using MATLAB with the complete design implementation. The secondary state equation of the linear acceleration PID function is the sum of Equations 3, 4, and 5 formulated in Equations 15 and 16. The quadratic Equation 21 is replaced by the linear acceleration term, and the remaining nonlinear differential equations are integrated as uniformly to describe the state equation. The implementation of the numerical acceleration model (directional vibration) used for linear acceleration PID functions is shown in Figure 4.

### 4.2.2 Efficiency Improvement by designing the Wheel Dynamics Model to Include the Linear Acceleration Variables

By replacing the nonlinear torque (\(T\)) and acceleration terms with the differential equation of the wheel dynamics, it is possible to gain variables for steady-state linear acceleration PID control performance, particularly highlighting the nonlinear role options in sensor measurement design for ratchet compensations [12], as Figure 5 presents. Recent studies have focused prominently on creating new functions for PID performance to guarantee optimal design exponents in clutches and tap reducers [26, 29, 32].

It is noted that the acceptable torque speed \(\omega_{\text{max}}\) required for optimal control performance of the control variable varies along the dimensionless conveying speed \(\omega x\). When \(\alpha = 1/2\), the torque \(\omega_{\text{max}}\) is identical to the maximum rate of change \(\alpha \cdot \omega x\), while when \(\alpha = 0\), a deceleration is necessary to attain \(\omega_{\text{max}}\). Such an aspect is reminiscent of the relationship between the applied torque time history and the average engine speed \(\dot{\omega}\) in the case of ratchet applications, as shown in Equation 12. The specification for accelerations limited to values such as 0.05, in the case of ratchet applications, works effectively for controller design, and the following formula ensures the smooth transfer of motion while refractoriness is still maintained.

### 3. Controller Design

The fault-tolerant super twisting sliding mode control is proposed to track the given altitude and attitude references in case of 60% actuator failure at one rotor. The control allocation algorithm is activated when one of the four rotors fails and enables the quadrotor to follow the references stably.

#### 3.1. Super Twisting Sliding Mode Controller

The sliding mode controller design is more robust than other controller methods in the literature. Two stages are very important in the sliding mode controller approach.

1) The selection of the sliding surface  
2) State variables must remain on the sliding surface  

The sliding phase and the reaching phase of the sliding mode controller are represented in Fig. 4 and the sliding surface is defined in (13) [39].

\[
s = \hat{e} + \lambda e \tag{13}
\]

where \( e \) is the error and \( \lambda \) represents the tuning parameter.

The sliding variables used in the sliding mode controller are given in (14).

\[
s^T = [\varphi \theta \psi z] \tag{14}
\]

The sliding variables must reach the sliding surface in finite time and slide on the surface to reach 0 asymptotically with the aim of controlling the quadrotor to the reference trajectory [40].

**4. Free Response Due to the Rotor Motion**In the next section, we will discuss the free response caused by the rotor motion. The rotor consists of a main rotor and a tail rotor, which operate continuously as the rocket spirals toward the ground. They are stationary with respect to the earth throughout the launch or flight. The rigid rotors do not generate significant vibration to the cabin of the spacecraft; however, due to the rapid rotation, the mass of each rotor is also much higher than that of the aircraft, thus greatly increasing the inertia at the wheels. This is one of the major factors that limit the control of the main rotor position in an envelope. On the other hand, the duel-axis tail rotor has a smaller flexibility than the main rotor. The moment of this rotor in the lateral direction is also small, thus, it can be controlled with less efforts, with the use of elevator angle actuators. On the other hand, its primary contribution to the vehicle ride is the motor thrust. The tail rotor is very small and is placed at the rear of the aircraft more than two times in size; if it were located at the front, the tail would mainly act as an unbalanced mass, which would make it difficult to control the lateral motion of the aircraft.

The fault-tolerant super twisting sliding mode controller diagram is represented in Fig. 7. Sliding mode control is a variable structure control method. The state feedback control law is not a continuous function of time. It can switch from one continuous structure to another continuous structure based on the current position in the state space [42], [43]. The sliding variable must be used to define the sliding surface. The reference trajectory is the trajectory given for the quadrotor to follow. The quadrotor tries to follow this trajectory using the sliding mode controller. When an actuator error occurs, and power loss occurs in one of the rotors, the control allocation mechanism is activated. It readjusts the power distribution between the rotors and keeps the quadrotor flying stably.

**Fig. 7.** Block scheme of the proposed controller

**4. Result and Discussions**In this part, the efficiency of the proposed fault-tolerant super-twisting sliding mode controller is verified by MATLAB simulations. The physical parameters of the quadrotor defined in the second section are used in the MATLAB simulations. An actuator fault due to 60% power loss in the fourth rotor is introduced at the beginning of the simulation. Simulations were made separately for cases with and without actuator failure. In this way, it has been observed more clearly how tolerant the proposed controller is against actuator errors. Fig. 8-11 shows the roll, pitch, yaw and altitude tracking responses of the controller without actuator failure.

### Page 10

ather on my site.The figure illustrates two example failure modes of the robot system controlled using natural language commands, specifically the "picture" reference tracking command. The primary focus is to demonstrate how the robot executes when the reference changes without the control system perceiving the change.

1. **Roll Angle Reference Tracking Failure (Figure a)**:
   - The graph in Figure a shows the roll angle reference tracking of the servomotor without failure.
   - The rotor angle values are plotted against the reference, which is user-input of the roller reference.
   - The PID controller adjusts the position of the servomotor to match the roller reference.
   - The trajectory of the servomotor's angle remains close to the desired roll angle, even when the roller angle changes.

2. **Pitch Angle Reference Tracking Failure (Figure b)**:
   - The graph in Figure b shows the pitch angle reference tracking of the servomotor without failure.
   - The rotor angle values are plotted against the reference, which is user-input of the pilot angle reference.
   - The PID controller adjusts the position of the servomotor's motor to match the pilot angle reference.
   - The trajectory of the servo's angle closely follows the desired pitch angle, even when the pilot angle is altered.

**Summary**:
- The servomotors in the system are controlled using natural language commands for both the angle and position.
- The roll and pitch angle references are defined by servomotor angular positions and adjustments are made using PID controllers.
- Despite the horizon of reference changes, the controllers are able to track these references accurately, demonstrating the robustness of the natural language interface and PID controllers in handling dynamic changes in the control system.

23. The engineering model was filled with a porous medium with a specified mass density, and the analysis showed that the control algorithm was able to track the expected trajectory accurately, indicating that it effectively controlled the rover to its desired path.

Another control method using a continuous-time Markov model (CTMM) was tested, but it was found that this method did not produce accurate predictions of the robot's movement on a rough terrain. The experiments conducted on laboratory control of a lunar exploration rover showed that the continuous-time Markov model and standard iterative methods of parameter estimation could not effectively track the robot's movement in the actual planetary environment. In contrast, particle filter-based controllers were shown to nearly accurately track the target trajectory, indicating that the controller was able to execute challenging tasks such as strict terrain evolution and failure detection, even under adverse conditions.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates the importance of considering and planning for key aspects of control for planetary exploration missions. For instance, developing/using error models that include knowledge of potential disturbance sources such as terrain evolution is critical for accurate estimation of control over time and robust diagnosis of large-scale disturbance events, such as failures of tools. A future research direction should be to study a network-based control method, in which multiple models are exercised for higher accuracy.

Figure 13. Altitude reference tracking simulation of the controller with rotor failure.
--
Table 3 gives the time response (rise time, overshoot and settling time) values of the controller with rotor failure. When the time response data in Table 3 is examined, it is seen that the rotor error increases the overshoot. However, it is not high enough to prevent the quadrotor from flying stably. The settling time is slightly longer than when there is no rotor error. However, the reference value is captured at around 0.6 seconds for roll, pitch and altitude references. The yaw reference can be captured in about 1 second. The system has a short settling time despite rotor failure.

As discussed in [BM6], the EDM has excluded from the context model expression. Thus, the ED models are written as bilinear interaction models and TOM methods (see Section 2.2.2) allow alternative expressions for the independent variables (e.g., (9)).

We study the performance of the ED and TOM models of a variety of explicative variables (species, etc.) and compare them to the result obtained by using the original Scikit estimate model (Eq. (7)) and the reduced ED estimates (Eq. (11)), where the ED analysis (Eq. (6)) is used (see also Eq. (4)). The reduced ED models are obtained using XGBoost and AT with the SMACD model (Eq. (15).

In Tab. 4, we compare the ED and TOM results (which are obtained using model (11)) to the ED model (Eq. (9)) and the original model (Eq. (7)). The ED estimate has high accuracy (meaning a small difference between original and TOM models).

The greatest drawbacks of the EDM model are the relatively high variance of the estimate. The authors suggest constructing the ED model in a hierarchical, multi-dimensional setting of ED and arbitrary Sobol composite functions G, T, S, throughout the entire vector of parameters.

**Conclusions:**

**Summary**

The ED model results indicate that the SFC did not result in very significant improvement in the structure of the vessel tree. Introducing new tree analysis indicators and widely available high quality trees can be a part of improving the model.
